data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's argument rests on an undefended equivocation between 'omitted cues' and 'uncodifiable cues.' The mechanism asserts that the checklist 'may fail to include these high-diagnostic cues' and that this loss of valid cue information offsets the panel's noise-cancellation advantage. But the question asks for an evaluation that distinguishes a genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer. SRC_001's distinction criterion is cue-selection accuracy, yet within a single evaluation it cannot separate a panel that is genuinely extracting diagnostic signal via checklist-mediated attention from one that coincidentally gets the answer right — it simply assumes that any checklist victory is compliance rather than genuine gain. Worse, SRC_001's own countercondition (dynamic checklist incorporating the expert's cues) concedes that the cue-omission explanation is not inherent to the panel-vs-expert comparison but is contingent on checklist quality, which leaves no domain-general evidence standard that privileges the expert without circularly assuming the checklist is inferior.
